questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: How is Social Security mainly paid for?

choices.text: Profits the government earns from the stock market
Payroll taxes on workers' wages and employers
Federal income tax on all income

questions.correct_answer: Payroll taxes on workers' wages and employers
questions.intro: Social Security is a federal program that pays retirement, disability, and survivor benefits. It is funded mainly by payroll taxes: workers pay 6.2% of wages (up to a yearly limit), and employers pay a matching 6.2%.
questions.feedback: Payroll taxes from workers and employers fund it.

misconceptions.B: Confuses Social Security with an investment fund
misconceptions.D: Confuses payroll tax with income tax

questions.prompt: Workers earn up to 4 Social Security credits per year and generally need 40 credits to qualify for retirement benefits. What is the fewest years of work needed?
questions.intro: Credits are earned by working and paying Social Security taxes. You can earn at most 4 credits per year, and you generally need 40 credits for retirement benefits.

questions.prompt: Tia's full retirement age is 67, when her benefit would be $1,800 a month. Claiming at 62 reduces it by 30%. What would she receive at 62?
questions.intro: Full retirement age is 67 for people born in 1960 or later. You can claim as early as 62, but the monthly benefit is permanently reduced (about 30% at 62). Waiting past full retirement age raises it.

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: What is a defined-benefit pension?

choices.text: A personal savings account that you invest yourself
A government benefit every worker gets
An annuity you buy with your own savings
A plan that promises a set monthly payment in retirement, often based on salary and years worked

questions.correct_answer: A plan that promises a set monthly payment in retirement, often based on salary and years worked
questions.intro: A defined-benefit (DB) pension promises a set payment based on a formula, and the employer bears the investment risk. A defined-contribution (DC) plan, such as a 401(k), depends on what is contributed and how investments perform; the worker bears the risk.
questions.feedback: DB pensions promise a formula-based payment.

misconceptions.B: Confuses a pension with Social Security
misconceptions.C: Confuses an employer promise with a purchase
